title: Measuring Clock Precision Without an Ideal Time Reference
authors: Pablo Á. Domínguez, Christopher Chubb, Mischa P. Woods
abstract: Characterising physical devices typically requires comparison with more precise reference standards. For clocks, however, this approach is problematic because no physically perfect time reference exists; real clocks have finite, model-dependent uncertainty. We address whether multiple imperfect clocks can collectively determine their precision without an absolute reference. This paper provides analytic bounds and protocols for quantifying clock precision using only multiple copies of the same clock, which need not be synchronised and may have manufacturing variations or environmental coupling. Beyond clock characterisation, these methods enable precise measurements f sub-period intervals and relativistic effects such as time dilation and Doppler shifts, providing tools for quantum metrology and fundamental physics.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to determine the precision of physical clocks using only multiple copies of the clock itself, bypassing the need for an ideal external time standard. It derives rigorous mathematical bounds connecting theoretical precision measures ($R$) to experimentally measurable quantities ($E[	au]$). This work provides novel tools for quantum metrology and fundamental physics measurements.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to quantify the intrinsic precision of physical clocks without relying on an ideal or external time reference.
main_result: It establishes analytic bounds and protocols showing that clock precision, characterized by $R$, can be inferred operationally using only multiple copies of the same clock.
method: The analysis employs advanced stochastic processes, renewal theory, and martingale techniques to relate theoretical precision measures to experimentally measurable quantities derived from multiple clock ticks.
model_or_system: The system models clocks as devices emitting time information via discrete, independently distributed 'ticks' with a measurable mean ($\mu$) and variance ($\sigma^2$).
key_observables: Clock precision ($R = \mu^2/\sigma^2$), Allan deviation ($\sigma_A(	au)$), and an experimentally derived figure of merit $E[	au]$ from double-tick measurements.
important_parameters: The number of clock copies ($N$), the measurement time interval ($	au$), and the initial offset ($\Delta$ or $\delta$).
main_assumptions: The tick intervals are assumed to be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), and the results often rely on asymptotic limits (e.g., $N 	o \infty$ or $R 	o \infty$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the general concept of clock ticks; Figure 2 details the double-tick experiment used to define the operational measurement $E[	au]$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the fundamental problem (lack of ideal reference) to introducing theoretical bounds ($R$), developing operational measurements ($E[	au]$) using multiple copies, and finally deriving rigorous asymptotic theorems relating these quantities.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework developed for characterizing fundamental physical constants (like time) using only internal statistical properties is highly relevant to quantum metrology and the theoretical limits of measurement in quantum optics.

FIG. 2. Experiment that defines the figure of merit E[τ] as in [20]. The two copies of the clock are started with an initial delay ∆= δµ, and they tick freely in an alternating manner. Due to the stochastic nature of the ticking period, one will almost surely find a situation in which one of the two copies produces two consecutive ticks without the other copy performing any ticks: a double tick. At that moment, we record the number of ticks that took place until then, denoted by τ, and we stop and reset the experiment.
